Human sa nahitabo nga kaylap nga pagbaha sa dakong bahin sa Luzon niining bag-ohay nga mga adlaw, gimando ni Pangulong Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. ang hugot nga pagpatuman sa mga balaod nga may kalabotan sa urban planning, ilabi na sa mga kritikal nga lugar sa tibuok nasod nga kanunay gibahaan. Sa gipahigayon nga media conference niining Martes, Septyembre 1, miingon si Palace Press Officer Atty. Claire Castro nga kini nga paghugot sa pagpatuman sa balaod sa urban planning gihisgutan sa miting ni PBBM uban sa nagkalain-laing ahensya sa gobyerno nga nangita og solusyon sa dakong problema sa pagbaha sa Metro Manila ug ubang mga lugar. “Kung nasunod lamang daw ang mga ito ay maaaring ang mga lugar na dapat tayuan ng mga imprastraktura at mga lugar na bahain ang dapat manatiling libre at walang imprastrakctura para siya ang tumanggap ng tubig-ulan,” giit ni Castro. Matud niya, adunay mga master plan na sa urban development nga nahimo alang sa Metro Manila sukad pa niadtong 1941 ug 1956 alang sa Cebu apan wala kini mapatuman, hinungdan nga nakatukod og mga imprastraktura ug mga puy-anan sa mga lugar nga nakasamok sa hapsay nga pag-agos sa tubig gikan sa mga suba ug estero. “Huwag nang mamulitika. Ipatupad na ang batas. A SEA OF TRASH FLOODS THE RIVER BESIDE BACLARAN CHURCH A massive accumulation of garbage from Manila Bay filled the river in front of Baclaran Church in Parañaque City on Monday, August 10, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or Habagat swept debris into the area. The thick layer of floating waste created an alarming scene, with trash covering a large portion of the waterway. Nearby residents said they had never experienced anything like this before, highlighting the unusual scale of the debris buildup following the heavy rainfall. The incident once again raises concerns about waste management, waterways, and the impact of heavy rains on communities near Manila Bay. August 29, 2026 — One can scarcely imagine the terror: standing inside your own home, hearing the roar of water, mud, and rocks approaching — and having only seconds to wonder if your family will survive. That was the reality for communities along the Nepal–Tibet border on August 26, 2026, when a massive glacier and rock collapse triggered a catastrophic flash flood along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers. Homes, roads, bridges, power plants, and entire settlements were swept away — often with little or no warning.  IN THOSE FINAL MOMENTS Residents were forced to scramble to rooftops, balconies, or any higher ground available — clinging to hope as waters rose nearly 30 feet in half an hour. We may never fully know what went through their minds: Were they crying? Calling loved ones? Praying? Holding each other? What we do know is that behind every statistic is a human life, a family, and a story of heartbreak.  THE SCALE OF LOSS - 469 confirmed dead — and still rising - Hundreds more remain missing, including tourists and pilgrims from several nations - Entire communities buried under mud and debris - Rescue teams continue to reach isolated areas "Behind every number is a family waiting. #1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. ₱47-M Flood Control Project in Laoag Collapses — Ties Emerge Between  Contractor Linked to Davao Lawmaker and Sandro Marcos’ Office A newly built flood control structure along Padsan River in Barangay Gabu, Laoag City — a project worth ₱47,024,704.34 funded under the 2024 General Appropriations Act (GAA) — has collapsed JUST MONTHS after its reported completion, sparking fresh outrage over the alleged “flood-control mafia” operating in Congress. Photos taken on-site show large concrete revetments cracked, dislodged, and washed into the river, exposing reinforcing steel and leaving the riverbank vulnerable to further erosion.  The project billboard names RA Pahati Construction & Supply, Inc. as the contractor, under the DPWH Ilocos Norte First District Engineering Office, with a target completion date of October 4, 2024. RA Pahati Construction is reportedly owned by the family of Rep. Jhong Ceniza of Pantukan, Davao de Oro — a name that has repeatedly surfaced in infrastructure procurement circles.  Sources familiar with congressional contracting allege that RA Pahati has become a favored builder for Rep. Sandro Marcos, the Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative, allegedly with some help from his chief of staff, said to be a relative of Rep. Ceniza’s wife. Residents and local engineers have raised alarm over the collapse, noting that the structure failed despite relatively moderate river flow in recent weeks. Infrastructure experts point out that proper soil compaction, adequate riprap foundation, and correct steel reinforcement are crucial in river dike construction — all of which appear deficient in the broken sections. The collapse has revived long-circulating allegations about flood control allocations being used as a “cash cow” for certain districts.  RA Pahati, controlled by the Ceniza family, has reportedly bagged billions in contracts across Luzon and Mindanao, despite originating from Davao de Oro. In Ilocos Norte, whispers persist that Rep. Sandro Marcos’ chief of staff — reportedly related by marriage to the Cenizas — has been instrumental in channeling projects to RA Pahati, bypassing stricter vetting.  Political analysts warn this could become a serious governance issue for the presidential son, especially as calls mount for greater transparency in the use of massive DPWH flood control budgets. The incident adds to the growing backlash against multi-billion flood control projects nationwide, long suspected to be overpriced, poorly built, and politically manipulated.  In Congress, several lawmakers — particularly from Mindanao — have been calling out selective investigations that spare politically allied districts while targeting rivals. Observers warn that this Laoag project could become a flashpoint, especially since it sits in the home turf of the President’s son, who is expected to champion good governance but now faces scrutiny over his district’s infrastructure spending. DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. So before anyone points a finger at Davao, perhaps we should remember that flooding is not a problem exclusive to one city. Water does not check political affiliations before it rises. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. For the past 15 years, I have had the privilege of traveling around Davao for team-building activities, retreats, seminars, workshops, and speaking engagements. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth. So if someone wants to call Davao the “Flood Capital of the Philippines,” perhaps we shouldn't be offended. Maybe we should simply redefine the flood. It is more precise as it utilizes Doppler radar technology to track real-time rainfall intensity, making it highly effective for immediate decision-making in flood-prone areas. 𝐓𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐍𝐀𝐍: Itutulad ng DPWH sa mga gagawing detention basins sa Pangasinan ang detention basin sa ilalim ng Metropolitan Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist sa Dagupan upang magkaroon ng imbakan ng tubig sa probinsya upang maibsan ang matinding baha tuwing malakas ang ulan. Kasunod ito ng utos ni Pangulong Ferdinand Marcos Jr. na magtayo ng mga water detention basins upang maibsan ang matinding pagbaha sa mga low-lying at flood-prone areas. Ininspeksyon ni Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon nitong Huwebes ang cathedral kasama sina Archbishop Socrates Villegas, Pangasinan 4th District Representative Gina De Venecia at Dagupan Vice Mayor Dean Bryan Kua, kung saan sinabi ng Kalihim na patuloy nakikipagtulungan ang ahensya sa mga Civil Society Organizations at local government units para sa dredging ng Sinocalan River, pagkukumpuni ng mga flood gates, at paglalagay ng sheetpiles sa Brgy. Caranglaan, at paglalagay ng mga mobile pumps, upang maprotektahan ang mga barangay ng Lasip Chico, Bacayo Sur, Lasip Grande, Pogo Grande, at mga karatig-lugar.
